opus-5.5.text:
Thanks, it's great to be here.

The way I think about Multipath Reliable Connection is that it starts from a simple observation: the networks we build for large-scale training don't look like the networks the traditional transport protocols were designed for. In a big AI cluster you have a huge number of GPUs doing collective operations: all-reduce, all-to-all, and so on. They all tend to send at the same time, in very synchronized bursts, and the whole job moves at the speed of the slowest flow. So tail latency isn't a nice-to-have metric. It directly determines how much of that very expensive hardware is actually doing useful work.

Classic RDMA transports, like RoCE, basically pin each connection to a single path through the network. Flow-level ECMP hashing then decides which path that is, and with a relatively small number of very large flows you get collisions. Two elephant flows land on the same link while other links sit idle, and suddenly your collective is waiting on the one congested path. People have tried to paper over that with careful traffic engineering, or by building networks with enough headroom that it mostly doesn't matter. Neither scales very gracefully.

What MRC does differently is spread a single connection's packets across many paths at once. It sprays them across the fabric so you're using the full bisection bandwidth the network actually has, rather than whatever subset the hash function happens to give you. Once you do that, a lot of things have to change at the transport layer. Packets arrive out of order, so you need to deliver them directly into memory without assuming in-order arrival. Loss detection has to tell the difference between a packet that's just taken a slower path and one that's genuinely gone. Congestion control has to work across a set of paths rather than just one. And you want to be able to notice that a particular path is bad, maybe because a link is flapping or a switch is misbehaving, and steer traffic away from it quickly.

That last point matters a lot at this scale. When you have tens of thousands of links, something is always failing somewhere. If the transport can route around failures on the timescale of round-trip times, rather than waiting for the routing system to reconverge or for an operator to intervene, the job just keeps going. That's a big part of the value: not only higher peak throughput, but much more predictable performance and resilience when things go wrong.

I'd also say a lot of these ideas aren't brand new. Multipath transport, packet spraying, receiver-driven approaches, trimming packets instead of dropping them: these have been explored in the research community for over a decade, including work I was involved with, like MPTCP and NDP. What's exciting now is that the economics of AI have made it worth actually building this into hardware and deploying it at enormous scale, and doing it in a way that's compatible with Ethernet and the broader Ultra Ethernet ecosystem rather than needing a completely proprietary fabric.

So my short answer is that MRC lets the network behave much more like one big, well-balanced pipe instead of a collection of individual paths that can each become a bottleneck. For synchronized AI workloads, that's exactly the property you want.

r001.rationale: The response says these ideas “aren't brand new” and describes them as techniques explored in prior research.

r002.rationale: It says the transport can route around failures and keep the job going, but does not explain that each flow traversing the failed component is affected only slightly.

r003.rationale: It says the transport can route around failures on the timescale of round-trip times and steer traffic away from a bad path quickly.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. The way I'd frame it is that AI clusters broke the assumptions that classic RDMA transports were built on. InfiniBand and RoCE were designed around a single path, in-order delivery, and a network that's mostly well behaved. Then you take tens of thousands of GPUs, connect them with a Clos fabric that has an enormous number of parallel paths, and run collectives like all-reduce and all-to-all that light up every link at once. Suddenly the transport is the thing holding you back. A single flow pinned to one path by ECMP hashing collides with other flows, you get hotspots, and one slow link stalls the whole collective because everything is synchronous.

Multipath Reliable Connection, MPRC, is essentially saying: let's stop pretending there's one path. Spray packets across all the available paths at fine granularity, do it from the NIC so you're not dependent on the switches getting the hashing right, and then handle the consequence, which is that packets arrive out of order. That out-of-order piece is the hard part and it's where most of the engineering goes. You need the receiver to be able to place data directly into memory regardless of arrival order, and you need loss recovery and congestion control that work per-packet rather than per-flow, because a loss on one path shouldn't tear down the whole connection or trigger go-back-N retransmissions that waste a huge amount of bandwidth.

The contribution, in my view, is two things. First, it drives link utilisation up and tail latency down, and for AI training tail latency is everything. You're waiting for the slowest participant, so the ninety-ninth percentile is really your effective throughput. Second, it makes the fabric more resilient. If a link flaps or degrades, traffic just naturally flows around it, rather than a static route sitting on a bad link until someone intervenes.

Where I'd be careful is not to oversell any single transport. Multipath transport only helps if the congestion control and the load balancing are designed together. If you spray packets but your congestion signal still thinks in terms of one path, you just move the problem around. And the ecosystem matters: this has to work across vendors, which is why you see efforts like Ultra Ethernet trying to standardise the ideas rather than leave each company with its own flavour. But the core shift, moving from single-path reliable connections to genuinely multipath ones, is one of the more important changes in datacentre networking in a long time, and it's being driven almost entirely by what AI workloads demand.

r001.rationale: The response describes MPRC’s mechanisms and calls the shift important, but does not say it combines previously invented techniques or characterize it as not fundamentally new.

r002.rationale: It says traffic flows around a flapping or degraded link, but does not explain that a failure only slightly affects every MPRC flow crossing that component.

r003.rationale: The response gives no timeframe for avoiding a failed link, such as within a few network round-trip times.

astra-6.text:
I see Multipath Reliable Connection as a way to make the network behave more like one large pool of capacity. In an AI supercomputer, you have many accelerators communicating at very high rates, and the workload often progresses only when the slowest transfer finishes. So an imbalance in the network can hold up a much larger computation.

There are usually multiple paths between the communicating machines. The challenge is to use those paths effectively while still providing reliable delivery. If you can spread traffic across them and adapt when a path becomes congested or fails, you can make better use of the capacity you’ve already built.

Of course, spreading packets across paths introduces complications: packets can arrive out of order, and you need to handle loss without creating unnecessary retransmissions or overwhelming the receiver. That’s where the transport design matters. The contribution is to make that complexity manageable, so the accelerators spend less time waiting for communication and more time doing useful work.

r001.rationale: The response describes Multipath Reliable Connection as managing traffic across multiple paths, but does not say it combines previously invented techniques or characterize it as not fundamentally new.

r002.rationale: It mentions adapting when a path fails, but does not explain that a network failure would only slightly affect flows traversing the failed component.

r003.rationale: It does not state that the connection stops using a failed link within a few network round-trip times.

sol-6.1.text:
I think its main contribution is to make the network’s multiple paths useful to a single communication. In an AI supercomputer, you don’t just need a lot of bandwidth in aggregate; you need that bandwidth available to the particular transfers happening right now. If a large transfer is pinned to one path, it can be held up by congestion while capacity elsewhere sits idle.

Multipath Reliable Connection lets you spread that traffic across paths while still providing reliable delivery. The challenge is handling packets arriving out of order and recovering from loss without making the whole transfer wait unnecessarily.

That matters because AI training is often synchronized: a late transfer can leave a lot of expensive accelerators waiting. So the benefit isn’t simply higher average throughput. It’s more consistent completion times, better use of the fabric, and greater resilience when a link or a path has a problem.

r001.rationale: The response describes using multiple paths for reliable delivery but does not characterize the approach as a combination of previously invented techniques.

r002.rationale: It mentions resilience to a link or path problem, but does not explain that only flows traversing the failed component are likely to be affected slightly.

r003.rationale: The response does not state how quickly Multipath Reliable Connection stops using a failed link.
